<div class="ri-item ri-informational">
  <div class="ri-key">0717</div>
  <div class="cell">This code is for backwards compatibility only as of v2.9. <span class="ws" title="line break">&#182;</span><br>If no restrictions, don’t send an ARV segment altogether.<span class="ws" title="2 spaces">&middot;&middot;</span>If sent, ARV-3 is a required element however. To emulate 0717 “NONE”, populate ARV-3 with code from new ActCode_ActPolicyType__ActInformationPolicy such as OrgNSI (organizational non-sensitive information policy) or PersNSI (personal non-sensitive information policy).<span class="ws" title="3 spaces">&middot;&middot;&middot;</span><span class="ws" title="line break">&#182;</span><br>Don’t populate ARV-7.<span class="ws" title="2 spaces">&middot;&middot;</span>E.g., Device record that is not sensitive. If you have a situation where an ARV-4 is valued, as required by, e.g., an organizational policy related to disclosure of<span class="ws" title="2 spaces">&middot;&middot;</span>a VIP’s health status or location at a facility, and the VIP has authorized disclosure as public information, one may use OrgPI (organizational public information policy - Organizational policy on collection, access, use, or disclosure of public information as defined by the organization or governing jurisdiction) to value ARV-3 indicating that the policy permits the disclosure of VIP sensitive information as coded in ARV-4.</div>
  <div class="ri-who">As emitted — outstanding site marked: <div class="cell">This code is for backwards compatibility only as of v2.9. <span class="ws" title="line break">&#182;</span><br>If no restrictions, don’t send an ARV segment altogether.<span class="ws" title="2 spaces">&middot;&middot;</span>If sent, ARV-3 is a required element however. To emulate 0717 “NONE”, populate ARV-3 with code from new ActCode_ActPolicyType__ActInformationPolicy such as OrgNSI (organizational non-sensitive information policy) or PersNSI (personal non-sensitive information policy).<span class="ws" title="3 spaces">&middot;&middot;&middot;</span><span class="ws" title="line break">&#182;</span><br>Don’t populate ARV-7.<span class="ws" title="2 spaces">&middot;&middot;</span>E.g., Device record that is not sensitive. If you have a situation where an ARV-4 is valued, as required by, e.g., an organizational policy related to disclosure of<span class="ws" title="2 spaces">&middot;&middot;</span>a VIP’s health status or location at a facility, and the VIP has authorized disclosure as public information, one may use OrgPI (organizational public information policy - Organizational policy on collection, access, use, or disclosure of public information as defined by the organization or governing jurisdiction) to value ARV-3 indicating that the policy permits the disclosure of VIP sensitive information as coded in ARV-4.</div></div>
</div>
<div class="ri-item ri-informational">
  <div class="ri-key">0717</div>
  <div class="cell">If the grantor&#x27;s term of agreement must be accepted in full, then this is considered &quot;&quot;basic consent&quot;&quot;. If a grantee is offered an opportunity to extend or restrict certain terms, then the agreement is considered &quot;&quot;granular consent&quot;&quot;.<span class="ws" title="line break">&#182;</span><br>Examples: (1) Healthcare: A PHR account holder [grantor] may require any PHR user [grantee] to accept the terms of agreement in full, or may permit a PHR user to extend or restrict terms selected by the account holder or requested by the PHR user. (2) Non-healthcare: The owner of a resource server [grantor] may require any authorization server [grantee] to meet authorization requirements stipulated in the grantor&#x27;s terms of agreement.</div>
  <div class="ri-who">As emitted — outstanding site marked: <div class="cell">If the grantor&#x27;s term of agreement must be accepted in full, then this is considered &quot;&quot;basic consent&quot;&quot;. If a grantee is offered an opportunity to extend or restrict certain terms, then the agreement is considered &quot;&quot;granular consent&quot;&quot;.<span class="ws" title="line break">&#182;</span><br>Examples: (1) Healthcare: A PHR account holder [grantor] may require any PHR user [grantee] to accept the terms of agreement in full, or may permit a PHR user to extend or restrict terms selected by the account holder or requested by the PHR user. (2) Non-healthcare: The owner of a resource server [grantor] may require any authorization server [grantee] to meet authorization requirements stipulated in the grantor&#x27;s terms of agreement.</div></div>
</div>
<div class="ri-item ri-informational">
  <div class="ri-key">0717</div>
  <div class="cell">Implied consent with no opportunity to assent or dissent to certain terms is considered &quot;&quot;basic consent&quot;&quot;.<span class="ws" title="line break">&#182;</span><br>Examples: (1) Healthcare: (a) A patient schedules an appointment with a provider, and either does not take the opportunity to expressly assent or dissent to the provider&#x27;s consent<span class="ws" title="2 spaces">&middot;&middot;</span>directive, does not have an opportunity to do so, as in the case where emergency care is required, or simply behaves as though the patient [grantor] agrees to the rights granted to the provider [grantee] in an implicit consent directive. (b) An injured and unconscious patient is deemed to have assented to emergency treatment by those permitted to do so under jurisdictional laws, e.g., Good Samaritan laws. (2) Non-healthcare: (a) Upon receiving a driver&#x27;s license, the driver is deemed to have assented without explicitly consenting to undergoing field sobriety tests. (b) A corporation that does business in a foreign nation is deemed to have deemed to have assented without explicitly consenting to abide by that nation&#x27;s laws.</div>
  <div class="ri-who">As emitted — outstanding site marked: <div class="cell">Implied consent with no opportunity to assent or dissent to certain terms is considered &quot;&quot;basic consent&quot;&quot;.<span class="ws" title="line break">&#182;</span><br>Examples: (1) Healthcare: (a) A patient schedules an appointment with a provider, and either does not take the opportunity to expressly assent or dissent to the provider&#x27;s consent<span class="ws" title="2 spaces">&middot;&middot;</span>directive, does not have an opportunity to do so, as in the case where emergency care is required, or simply behaves as though the patient [grantor] agrees to the rights granted to the provider [grantee] in an implicit consent directive. (b) An injured and unconscious patient is deemed to have assented to emergency treatment by those permitted to do so under jurisdictional laws, e.g., Good Samaritan laws. (2) Non-healthcare: (a) Upon receiving a driver&#x27;s license, the driver is deemed to have assented without explicitly consenting to undergoing field sobriety tests. (b) A corporation that does business in a foreign nation is deemed to have deemed to have assented without explicitly consenting to abide by that nation&#x27;s laws.</div></div>
</div>
<div class="ri-item ri-informational">
  <div class="ri-key">0717</div>
  <div class="cell">Implied or &quot;&quot;implicit&quot;&quot; consent with an &quot;&quot;opportunity to dissent&quot;&quot; occurs when the grantor&#x27;s behavior is understood by a reasonable person to signal assent to the grantee&#x27;s terms of agreement whether the grantor requests or the grantee approves further restrictions, is considered &quot;&quot;granular consent&quot;&quot;.<span class="ws" title="line break">&#182;</span><br> Examples: (1) Healthcare: (a) A healthcare provider deems a patient&#x27;s assent to disclosure of health information to family members and friends, but offers an opportunity or permits the patient to dissent to such disclosures.(b) A health information exchanges deems a patient to have assented to disclosure of health information for treatment purposes, but offers the patient an opportunity to dissents to disclosure to particular provider organizations. (2) Non-healthcare: A bank deems a banking customer&#x27;s assent to specified collection, access, use, or disclosure of financial information as a requirement of holding a bank account, but provides the user an opportunity to limit third-party collection, access, use or disclosure of that information for marketing purposes.</div>
  <div class="ri-who">As emitted — outstanding site marked: <div class="cell">Implied or &quot;&quot;implicit&quot;&quot; consent with an &quot;&quot;opportunity to dissent&quot;&quot; occurs when the grantor&#x27;s behavior is understood by a reasonable person to signal assent to the grantee&#x27;s terms of agreement whether the grantor requests or the grantee approves further restrictions, is considered &quot;&quot;granular consent&quot;&quot;.<span class="ws" title="line break">&#182;</span><br> Examples: (1) Healthcare: (a) A healthcare provider deems a patient&#x27;s assent to disclosure of health information to family members and friends, but offers an opportunity or permits the patient to dissent to such disclosures.(b) A health information exchanges deems a patient to have assented to disclosure of health information for treatment purposes, but offers the patient an opportunity to dissents to disclosure to particular provider organizations. (2) Non-healthcare: A bank deems a banking customer&#x27;s assent to specified collection, access, use, or disclosure of financial information as a requirement of holding a bank account, but provides the user an opportunity to limit third-party collection, access, use or disclosure of that information for marketing purposes.</div></div>
</div>
<div class="ri-item ri-informational">
  <div class="ri-key">0717</div>
  <div class="cell">The grantee&#x27;s terms of agreement, may be available to the grantor by reviewing the grantee&#x27;s privacy policies, but there is no notice by which a grantor is apprised of the policy directly or able to acknowledge.<span class="ws" title="line break">&#182;</span><br>Examples: (1) Healthcare: (a) Without notification or an opportunity to assent or dissent, a patient&#x27;s health information is automatically included in and available (often according to certain rules) through a health information exchange. Note that this differs from implied consent, where the patient is assumed to have consented. (b) Without notification or an opportunity to assent or dissent, a patient&#x27;s health information is collected, accessed, used, or disclosed for research, public health, security, fraud prevention, court order, or law enforcement. (2) Non-healthcare: (a) Without notification or an opportunity to assent or dissent, a consumer&#x27;s healthcare or non-healthcare internet searches are aggregated for secondary uses such as behavioral tracking and profiling. (b) Without notification or an opportunity to assent or dissent, a consumer&#x27;s location and activities in a shopping mall are tracked by RFID tags on purchased items</div>

(2) Non-healthcare: (a) Without notification or an opportunity to assent or dissent, a consumer&#x27;s healthcare or non-healthcare internet searches are aggregated for secondary uses such as behavioral tracking and profiling. (b) Without notification or an opportunity to assent or dissent, a consumer&#x27;s location and activities in a shopping mall are tracked by RFID tags on purchased items</div></div>
</div>
<div class="ri-item ri-informational">
  <div class="ri-key">0717</div>
  <div class="cell">Opt-in with no opportunity for a grantor to restrict certain permissions sought by the grantee is considered &quot;&quot;basic consent&quot;&quot;.<span class="ws" title="line break">&#182;</span><br>Examples: (1)<span class="ws" title="2 spaces">&middot;&middot;</span>Healthcare: A patient [grantor] signs a provider&#x27;s [grantee&#x27;s] consent directive form, which lists permissible collection, access, use, or disclosure activities, purposes of use, handling caveats, and revocation policies. (2) Non-healthcare: An employee [grantor] signs an employer&#x27;s [grantee&#x27;s] non-disclosure and non-compete agreement.</div>
  <div class="ri-who">As emitted — outstanding site marked: <div class="cell">Opt-in with no opportunity for a grantor to restrict certain permissions sought by the grantee is considered &quot;&quot;basic consent&quot;&quot;.<span class="ws" title="line break">&#182;</span><br>Examples: (1)<span class="ws" title="2 spaces">&middot;&middot;</span>Healthcare: A patient [grantor] signs a provider&#x27;s [grantee&#x27;s] consent directive form, which lists permissible collection, access, use, or disclosure activities, purposes of use, handling caveats, and revocation policies. <div class="ri-item ri-informational">
  <div class="ri-key">0717</div>
  <div class="cell">Opt-in with restrictions is considered &quot;&quot;granular consent&quot;&quot; because the grantor has an opportunity to narrow the permissions sought by the grantee.<span class="ws" title="line break">&#182;</span><br>Examples: (1) Healthcare: A patient assent to grantee&#x27;s consent directive terms for collection, access, use, or disclosure of health information, and dissents to disclosure to certain recipients as allowed by the provider&#x27;s pre-approved restriction list. (2) Non-healthcare: A cell phone user assents to the cell phone&#x27;s privacy practices and terms of use, but dissents from location tracking by turning off the cell phone&#x27;s tracking capability.</div>
  <div class="ri-who">As emitted — outstanding site marked: <div class="cell">Opt-in with restrictions is considered &quot;&quot;granular consent&quot;&quot; because the grantor has an opportunity to narrow the permissions sought by the grantee.<span class="ws" title="line break">&#182;</span><br>Examples: (1) Healthcare: A patient assent to grantee&#x27;s consent directive terms for collection, access, use, or disclosure of health information, and dissents to disclosure to certain recipients as allowed by the provider&#x27;s pre-approved restriction list. <div class="ri-item ri-informational">
  <div class="ri-key">0717</div>
  <div class="cell">Opt-out with no opportunity for a grantor to permit certain permissions sought by the grantee is considered &quot;&quot;basic consent&quot;&quot;.<span class="ws" title="line break">&#182;</span><br>Examples: (1) Healthcare: A patient [grantor] declines to sign a provider&#x27;s [grantee&#x27;s] consent directive form, which lists permissible collection, access, use, or disclosure activities, purposes of use, handling caveats, revocation policies, and consequences of not assenting. (2) Non-healthcare: (a)<span class="ws" title="2 spaces">&middot;&middot;</span>A patient [grantor] declines to sign a provider&#x27;s [grantee&#x27;s] consent directive form, which lists permissible collection, access, use, or disclosure activities, purposes of use, handling caveats, revocation policies, and consequences of not assenting. (b) A citizen [grantor] refuses to enroll in mandatory government [grantee] health insurance based on religious beliefs, which is an exemption.</div>

<div class="ri-item ri-informational">
  <div class="ri-key">0717</div>
  <div class="cell">Opt-out with exceptions is considered a &quot;&quot;granular consent&quot;&quot; because the grantor has an opportunity to accept certain permissions sought by the grantee or request additional grantor terms, while rejecting other grantee terms. <span class="ws" title="line break">&#182;</span><br>Examples: (1) Healthcare: A patient [grantor] dissents to a health information exchange consent directive with the exception of disclosure based on a limited &quot;&quot;time to live&quot;&quot; shared secret [e.g., a token or password], which the patient can give to a provider when seeking care. (2) Non-healthcare: A social media user [grantor] dissents from public access to their account, but assents to access to a circle of friends.</div>

<div class="ri-item ri-informational">
  <div class="ri-key">0717</div>
  <div class="cell">To specify the scope of an “EMRGONLY” consent directive within a policy domain, use one or more of the following Purpose of Use codes in the ActReason code system OID: 2.16.840.1.113883.5.8.<span class="ws" title="line break">&#182;</span><br>ETREAT (Emergency Treatment)<span class="ws" title="line break">&#182;</span><br>Description:<span class="ws" title="line break">&#182;</span><br>To perform one or more operations on information for provision of immediately needed health care for an emergent condition.<span class="ws" title="line break">&#182;</span><br>BTG (break the glass)<span class="ws" title="line break">&#182;</span><br>Description:<span class="ws" title="line break">&#182;</span><br>To perform policy override operations on information for provision of immediately needed health care for an emergent condition affecting potential harm, death or patient safety by end users who are not provisioned for this purpose of use. Includes override of organizational provisioning policies and may include override of subject of care consent directive restricting access.<span class="ws" title="line break">&#182;</span><br>ERTREAT (emergency room treatment)<span class="ws" title="line break">&#182;</span><br>Description:<span class="ws" title="line break">&#182;</span><br>To perform one or more operations on information for provision of immediately needed health care for an emergent condition in an emergency room or similar emergent care context by end users provisioned for this purpose, which does not constitute as policy override such as in a &quot;&quot;Break the Glass&quot;&quot; purpose of use.<span class="ws" title="line break">&#182;</span><br>THREAT (threat)<span class="ws" title="line break">&#182;</span><br>Description:<span class="ws" title="line break">&#182;</span><br>To perform one or more operations on information used to prevent injury or disease to living subjects who may be the target of violence.<span class="ws" title="line break">&#182;</span><br>DISASTER (disaster) <span class="ws" title="line break">&#182;</span><br>Description:<span class="ws" title="line break">&#182;</span><br>To perform one or more operations on information used for provision of immediately needed health care to a population of living subjects located in a disaster zone.<span class="ws" title="line break">&#182;</span><br>Map: An “emergency only” consent directive maps to ISO/TS 17975:2015(E)<span class="ws" title="line break">&#182;</span><br>5.13 Exceptional access.&quot;</div>

<div class="ri-item ri-informational">
  <div class="ri-key">0717</div>
  <div class="cell">A code representing U.S. Public Law 104-191 Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) Privacy Rule (45 CFR Section 164.508) Uses and disclosures for which an authorization is required https://www.gpo.gov/fdsys/pkg/CFR-2017-title45-vol1/pdf/CFR-2017-title45-vol1-sec164-508.pdf, which stipulates the process by which a covered entity seeks agreement from an individual to use or disclose protected health information for other purposes, or to authorize another covered entity to disclose protected health information to the requesting covered entity, are termed &quot;&quot;authorizations&quot;&quot;.<span class="ws" title="line break">&#182;</span><br><span class="ws" title="line break">&#182;</span><br>An “authorization” is required by the Privacy Rule for uses and disclosures of protected health information not otherwise allowed by the Rule. Where the Privacy Rule requires patient authorization, voluntary consent is not sufficient to permit a use or disclosure of protected health information unless it also satisfies the requirements of a valid authorization. An authorization is a detailed document that gives covered entities permission to use protected health information for specified purposes, which are generally other than treatment, payment, or health care operations, or to disclose protected health information to a third party specified by the individual.<span class="ws" title="line break">&#182;</span><br><span class="ws" title="line break">&#182;</span><br>An authorization must specify a number of elements, including a description of the protected health information to be used and disclosed, the person authorized to make the use or disclosure, the person to whom the covered entity may make the disclosure, an expiration date, and, in some cases, the purpose for which the information may be used or disclosed. With limited exceptions, covered entities may not condition treatment or coverage on the individual providing an authorization. https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/faq/264/what-is-the-difference-between-consent-and-authorization/index.html</div>
  <div class="ri-who">As emitted — outstanding site marked: <div class="cell">A code representing U.S. Public Law 104-191 Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) Privacy Rule (45 CFR Section 164.508) Uses and disclosures for which an authorization is required https://www.gpo.gov/fdsys/pkg/CFR-2017-title45-vol1/pdf/CFR-2017-title45-vol1-sec164-508.pdf, which stipulates the process by which a covered entity seeks agreement from an individual to use or disclose protected health information for other purposes, or to authorize another covered entity to disclose protected health information to the requesting covered entity, are termed &quot;&quot;authorizations&quot;&quot;.<span class="ws" title="line break">&#182;</span><br><span class="ws" title="line break">&#182;</span><br>An “authorization” is required by the Privacy Rule for uses and disclosures of protected health information not otherwise allowed by the Rule. Where the Privacy Rule requires patient authorization, voluntary consent is not sufficient to permit a use or disclosure of protected health information unless it also satisfies the requirements of a valid authorization. An authorization is a detailed document that gives covered entities permission to use protected health information for specified purposes, which are generally other than treatment, payment, or health care operations, or to disclose protected health information to a third party specified by the individual.<span class="ws" title="line break">&#182;</span><br><span class="ws" title="line break">&#182;</span><br>An authorization must specify a number of elements, including a description of the protected health information to be used and disclosed, the person authorized to make the use or disclosure, the person to whom the covered entity may make the disclosure, an expiration date, and, in some cases, the purpose for which the information may be used or disclosed. With limited exceptions, covered entities may not condition treatment or coverage on the individual providing an authorization. https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/faq/264/what-is-the-difference-between-consent-and-authorization/index.html</div></div>
</div>

  <div class="cell">Article 6.1.a https://gdpr-info.eu/art-6-gdpr/<span class="ws" title="line break">&#182;</span><br>1 Processing shall be lawful only if and to the extent that at least one of the following applies: (a) the data subject has given consent to the processing of his or her personal data for one or more specific purposes.<span class="ws" title="line break">&#182;</span><br>Article 9.1, 9.2a., 9.2.e https://gdpr-info.eu/art-9-gdpr/ <span class="ws" title="line break">&#182;</span><br>1. Processing of personal data revealing racial or ethnic origin, political opinions, religious or philosophical beliefs, or trade union membership, and the processing of genetic data, biometric data for the purpose of uniquely identifying a natural person, data concerning health or data concerning a natural person’s sex life or sexual orientation shall be prohibited.<span class="ws" title="line break">&#182;</span><br>2. Paragraph 1 shall not apply if one of the following applies: (a) the data subject has given explicit consent to the processing of those personal data for one or more specified purposes, except where Union or Member State law provide that the prohibition referred to in paragraph 1 may not be lifted by the data subject; and (e) processing relates to personal data which are manifestly made public by the data subject.&quot;</div>

  <div class="cell">Article 6.1.b https://gdpr-info.eu/art-6-gdpr/<span class="ws" title="line break">&#182;</span><br>1Processing shall be lawful only if and to the extent that at least one of the following applies: (b) processing is necessary for the performance of a contract to which the data subject is party or in order to take steps at the request of the data subject prior to entering into a contract.<span class="ws" title="line break">&#182;</span><br><span class="ws" title="line break">&#182;</span><br>Recital 44 https://gdpr-info.eu/recitals/no-44/<span class="ws" title="line break">&#182;</span><br>Processing should be lawful where it is necessary in the context of a contract or the intention to enter into a contract. * This title is an unofficial description.&quot;</div>
  <div class="ri-who">As emitted — outstanding site marked: <div class="cell">Article 6.1.b https://gdpr-info.eu/art-6-gdpr/<span class="ws" title="line break">&#182;</span><br>1Processing shall be lawful only if and to the extent that at least one of the following applies: (b) processing is necessary for the performance of a contract to which the data subject is party or in order to take steps at the request of the data subject prior to entering into a contract.<span class="ws" title="line break">&#182;</span><br><span class="ws" title="line break">&#182;</span><br>Recital 44 https://gdpr-info.eu/recitals/no-44/<span class="ws" title="line break">&#182;</span><br>Processing should be lawful where it is necessary in the context of a contract or the intention to enter into a contract. * This title is an unofficial description.&quot;</div></div>

<div class="ri-item ri-informational">
  <div class="ri-key">0717</div>
  <div class="cell">This processing policy code offers an escape-hatch to countries like Denmark and Austria: they simply declare their national healthcare data exchanges to be necessary for the management of their healthcare system. This allows them to establish an opt-out mechanism under the GDPR, whereas normally GDPR would be opt-in when it comes to such national exchanges.<span class="ws" title="line break">&#182;</span><br><span class="ws" title="line break">&#182;</span><br>The description is based on the following GDPR provisions:<span class="ws" title="line break">&#182;</span><br>Article 9.1, and 9.2.c and 9.2.h, 9.3 https://gdpr-info.eu/art-9-gdpr/<span class="ws" title="line break">&#182;</span><br>1. Processing of personal data revealing racial or ethnic origin, political opinions, religious or philosophical beliefs, or trade union membership, and the processing of genetic data, biometric data for the purpose of uniquely identifying a natural person, data concerning health or data concerning a natural person’s sex life or sexual orientation shall be prohibited.<span class="ws" title="line break">&#182;</span><br>2. Paragraph 1 shall not apply if one of the following applies: (c) processing is necessary to protect the vital interests of the data subject or of another natural person where the data subject is physically or legally incapable of giving consent; (h) processing is necessary for the purposes of preventive or occupational medicine, for the assessment of the working capacity of the employee, medical diagnosis, the provision of health or social care or treatment or the management of health or social care systems and services on the basis of Union or Member State law or pursuant to contract with a health professional and subject to the conditions and safeguards referred to in paragraph 3;<span class="ws" title="line break">&#182;</span><br>3. Personal data referred to in paragraph 1 may be processed for the purposes referred to in point (h) of paragraph 2 when those data are processed by or under the responsibility of a professional subject to the obligation of professional secrecy under Union or Member State law or rules established by national competent bodies or by another person also subject to an obligation of secrecy under Union or Member State law or rules established by national competent bodies.</div>

Paragraph 1 shall not apply if one of the following applies: (c) processing is necessary to protect the vital interests of the data subject or of another natural person where the data subject is physically or legally incapable of giving consent; (h) processing is necessary for the purposes of preventive or occupational medicine, for the assessment of the working capacity of the employee, medical diagnosis, the provision of health or social care or treatment or the management of health or social care systems and services on the basis of Union or Member State law or pursuant to contract with a health professional and subject to the conditions and safeguards referred to in paragraph 3;<span class="ws" title="line break">&#182;</span><br>3. Personal data referred to in paragraph 1 may be processed for the purposes referred to in point (h) of paragraph 2 when those data are processed by or under the responsibility of a professional subject to the obligation of professional secrecy under Union or Member State law or rules established by national competent bodies or by another person also subject to an obligation of secrecy under Union or Member State law or rules established by national competent bodies.</div></div>

<div class="ri-item ri-informational">

  <div class="cell">Superset—a set of batteries or procedures ordered under a single code unit but processed as separate batteries (e.g., routines = CBC, UA, electrolytes)<span class="ws" title="line break">&#182;</span><br>This set indicates that the code being described is used to order multiple service/test/observation batteries.<span class="ws" title="2 spaces">&middot;&middot;</span>For example, a client who routinely orders a CBC, a differential, and a thyroxine as an outpatient profile might use a single, special code to order all three test batteries, instead of having to submit three separate order codes.</div>
